title: YOU WILL EAT WHAT YOU PLANT
paragraphs: YOU WILL EAT WHAT YOU PLANT

“You reap what you sow” is not karma, not a threat that every tragedy is punishment, and not a cute motivational quote. In the hands of the apostle Paul, it is a warning about something frighteningly ordinary: the life you keep feeding is quietly becoming the life you will eventually have to live.
There are seeds in your life that nobody can see yet.
That is what should make you pause.

Not because God is waiting behind a corner to destroy you the moment you fail. Not because every painful thing happening to you is proof that you secretly deserved it. And certainly not because Christianity teaches some baptized version of karma.
It doesn’t.
But Scripture does teach something uncomfortable.
What you repeatedly plant matters.
The private compromise matters.
The resentment you keep watering matters.
The pornography you keep returning to matters.
The lie you have repeated so many times that it barely feels like lying anymore matters.
The unforgiveness you rehearse when nobody is listening matters.
The secret generosity matters too.
The prayer nobody applauds matters.
The temptation you resisted while your flesh screamed for satisfaction matters.
The apology that cost your pride matters.
The Scripture you opened when you wanted to scroll instead matters.
The quiet obedience nobody will ever post about matters.
Seeds are small.
Harvests are not.
And perhaps that is why these words from Paul should make every one of us stop:
“Μὴ πλανᾶσθε, Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται· ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.”
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε — Mē planasthe.
“Do not be deceived.”
Then:
Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται — Theos ou myktērizetai.
“God is not mocked.”
And then the principle:
ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.
“For whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
That is Galatians 6:7.
Notice where Paul begins.
Not with “reaping.”
With deception.
“Do not be deceived.”
Because one of sin’s greatest powers is not merely making evil attractive.
It is making consequences seem impossible.
Just once.
Nobody knows.
I can stop whenever I want.
God understands.
It isn't hurting anyone.
I'll repent later.
This is just who I am.
Everybody does it.
And little by little, what once disturbed your conscience becomes familiar enough to live with.
A seed disappears beneath the soil.
Nothing happens.
So you plant another.
Still nothing.
Another.
Nothing.
And because there is no immediate harvest, you begin to believe there never will be one.
That is the deception.
We often imagine consequences should arrive like lightning.
But seeds don't work like lightning.
They work underground.
Paul continues:
“For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (Galatians 6:8).
The Greek word translated “flesh” is σάρξ — sarx.

In this context, Paul is not saying that the physical human body is inherently evil. He is speaking about human life oriented away from God—the fallen self with its desires enthroned, the life that keeps saying, “My will. My appetite. My glory. My way.”
And there is something terrifying about feeding that life.
Whatever you feed grows stronger.
You don't usually wake up one morning and suddenly become bitter.
You rehearse offenses.
You replay conversations.
You assume motives.
You keep watering the wound.
Eventually bitterness stops feeling like something you carry.
It starts feeling like who you are.
You don't usually destroy a marriage in one afternoon.
You sow neglect.
You stop listening.
You hide things.
You entertain fantasies.
You make small compromises.
You protect your pride.
You keep planting.
Then one day everyone stares at the harvest and asks:
“How did we get here?”
Seeds.
You don't usually abandon your faith with one dramatic announcement.
Sometimes it happens one almost invisible decision at a time.
One prayer skipped.
Then another.
One compromise excused.
One conviction ignored.
One Sunday where Jesus can wait.
One month where Scripture stays closed.
One relationship that keeps pulling you away from Christ.
One secret you refuse to bring into the light.
Until eventually you look around and realize you have traveled much farther from Jesus than you ever intended.
Seeds.
But now we have to be very careful.
Because “you reap what you sow” has also been used cruelly.
Someone gets cancer: “You must have sown something.”
Someone loses a child: “You're reaping what you planted.”
Someone experiences abuse: “Maybe this is the consequence of your choices.”
No.
That is not faithful biblical interpretation.

Jesus Himself rejected simplistic equations between personal tragedy and personal guilt. In John 9, when His disciples encountered a man blind from birth, they asked whose sin caused his blindness—his or his parents'. Jesus refused their assumption.
And in Luke 13, when people told Jesus about Galileans whom Pilate had killed, Jesus did not tell the survivors, “They suffered because they were worse sinners.”
Scripture teaches sowing and reaping.
Scripture does not give you permission to stand over every suffering person and pretend you know why they are bleeding.
We live in a fallen world.
People suffer because of their own decisions.
People suffer because of other people's sins.
People suffer because creation itself is groaning under the curse of the Fall.
And sometimes we simply do not know why a particular tragedy happened.
So Galatians 6:7 is not a weapon for diagnosing somebody else's pain.
It is a mirror for examining your own life.
That changes everything.
Because suddenly the question isn't:
“What are they going to reap?”
It is:
“What am I planting?”
And that question can become painfully personal.
What are you planting in your marriage?
What are you planting in your children?
What are you planting into your mind at midnight when nobody else is watching?
What are you planting every time someone succeeds and jealousy rises inside you?
What are you planting through the words you speak about people who aren't in the room?
What are you planting with your money?
Your eyes?
Your time?
Your anger?
Your phone?
Your habits?
Your secret life?
If everything you repeatedly planted during the last year suddenly became visible as a harvest tomorrow morning...
would you want to eat it?
That question hurts.
It hurts me too.
Because none of us gets through Galatians 6 by pointing at everybody else.
We have all planted things we regret.
Some of us are living among the weeds right now.
Maybe you ignored the warnings.
Maybe you knew better.
Maybe God convicted you and you kept going.
Maybe the relationship collapsed.
Maybe trust disappeared.
Maybe addiction dug its roots deeper.
Maybe anger cost you people you loved.
Maybe years disappeared while you kept promising yourself that tomorrow would be different.
And now you are staring at consequences you cannot simply pray backward.
This is where people sometimes misunderstand grace.
We imagine grace means consequences magically disappear.
Sometimes God does mercifully remove consequences.
Sometimes He doesn't.
David was forgiven after his grievous sins, but forgiveness did not mean every earthly consequence vanished.
A thief can meet Jesus and still need to return what was stolen.
An adulterer can genuinely repent and still face shattered trust.
An addict can be forgiven completely and still need years of healing, accountability, and restoration.
Forgiveness is not God pretending the seed was never planted.
The Gospel is something even more astonishing.
God can meet you in the field you ruined.
Read that again.
God can meet you in the field you ruined.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of good farmers congratulating themselves on producing perfect crops.
It is the story of sinners who desperately needed a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
This is where “you reap what you sow” becomes far more profound than karma.
Karma says, in simplified popular usage, that your deeds return to you.
The Gospel announces that guilty people can receive mercy they did not earn because Jesus Christ bore judgment for sinners.
Scripture says:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The religious.
The rebellious.
The preacher.
The addict.
The person reading this with tears in their eyes.
The person reading this while hiding something nobody else knows.
If our hope were simply receiving exactly what our sins deserve, none of us could boast.
But the center of Christianity is a cross.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, was crucified.
Not because He needed forgiveness.
We did.
Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Paul says that God made Christ, who knew no sin, “to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
This is scandalous grace.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The unclean can be washed.
The wandering can come home.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
Not because sin didn't matter.
Look at the cross and try saying sin doesn't matter.
It mattered enough that redemption cost blood.
But look at the empty tomb before saying your story cannot change.
Jesus rose.
And because Christ lives, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That doesn't mean you can sow rebellion all week and casually sprinkle “grace” over it on Sunday.
Paul destroys that idea elsewhere:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” (Romans 6:1–2).
Grace is not permission to keep planting poison.
Grace takes the shovel out of your hand, calls you out of the field, forgives you, changes you, and teaches you to plant differently.
That is repentance.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward Christ today.
It is bringing the hidden thing into the light.
It is confessing.
It is surrendering.
It is saying:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living like this.”
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to say tonight.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
Maybe nobody knows what you're fighting.
Maybe everybody thinks you're strong.
Maybe your Facebook photos look happy.
Maybe you know how to say “God is good” while quietly wondering how much longer you can keep pretending.
Maybe you have become frighteningly skilled at appearing spiritually alive while starving inside.
Jesus already knows.
There is no room in your heart so dark that Christ has to discover it.
He knows.
And still He calls sinners to come.
Not to perform.
Not to hide.
To repent and believe.
So come.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with the consequences.
Come with the memories.
Come with the habit you swore you would never return to.
Come with the marriage you damaged.
Come with the pride you protected.
Come with the years you wasted.
Come with the field full of things you wish you had never planted.
But come to Jesus.
Because your past sowing may explain part of your present harvest, but in Christ it does not have sovereign authority over your eternal future.
Jesus does.
And now, by the Spirit, begin planting differently.
Paul does not end his teaching with despair.
Immediately after speaking about sowing to the Spirit, he says:
“And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).
Did you catch that?
Don't give up.
Perhaps you've been praying and seeing nothing.
Keep planting.
You've been trying to rebuild trust and it feels painfully slow.
Keep planting faithfulness.
You've been fighting temptation and nobody knows how difficult the battle has been.
Keep planting obedience.
You've been opening Scripture even though your emotions feel numb.
Keep planting truth.
You've been forgiving again and again.
Keep planting mercy.
You've been serving without recognition.
Keep planting love.
You've been praying for your child who seems farther from God than ever.
Keep praying.
You do not control the harvest.
God does.
Your calling is faithfulness.
Some seeds take time.
That truth cuts both ways.
It warns the person secretly sowing destruction:
Don't confuse delayed consequences with divine approval.
But it also comforts the exhausted believer sowing faithfulness:
Don't confuse delayed fruit with divine absence.
God sees what is underground.
So perhaps today is not merely another day.
Perhaps today is planting season.
You cannot crawl back into yesterday and remove every seed.
But because of Jesus, you can repent today.
You can confess today.
You can forgive today.
You can delete it today.
You can make the call today.
You can ask for help today.
You can open your Bible today.
You can return to church today.
You can tell the truth today.
You can kneel beside your bed tonight and finally stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Be honest.
If you're exhausted but still refusing to abandon Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if God has been rebuilding what sin, pain, or years of wandering damaged, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first time we stop pretending there isn't a struggle.
And please don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
There may be a night when temptation becomes louder than conviction, and you need to remember what kind of seed is sitting in your hand.
Christ alone is Lord, salvation is by grace, and Christians glorify God through lives surrendered to Him.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has been drifting.
Invite the believer who is tired.
Invite the person who thinks they have gone too far.
Invite even the person who doesn't yet believe.
Because somebody scrolling through your shared post may be holding a seed tonight.
A decision.
A temptation.
A secret.
A surrender.
And God may use one truth-filled article to make them stop before they plant something they will spend years wishing they could uproot.
Or perhaps the person holding that seed is you.
Then hear the warning.
But hear the Gospel too.
You will reap what you sow.
So stop planting what is killing you.
Run to Jesus.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And by the power of His Spirit, start planting what you will someday thank God you did.
Because the most breathtaking part of your story may not be the field you ruined...
but the Savior who walked into it and refused to leave you there.
